extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (especially Aristotelian ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and exposition of Aristotle's account of friendship, self-love, social bonds, and the relation of pleasure to the good life. Useful for producing essays, lectures, or summaries about virtue ethics and interpersonal goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-friendship requires internal harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: The wicked cannot be friends even to themselves because their soul is 'rent by faction' — one principle grieves at abstaining while another is pleased, so they cannot sympathise with themselves in joys and sorrows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-friendship demands unity of the soul and absence of remorse; being a friend to oneself follows from being good, since the good man has nothing inwardly to prevent self-regard as friendship. The passage contrasts internal division (wicked) with the self-sympathy of the good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kindly Feeling is distinct from Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Kindly Feeling may exist toward those we do not know and without their awareness; it lacks the intensity, yearning, and intimacy that Affection and true Friendship require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kindly Feeling can be a superficial, sudden liking (a 'dormant Friendship') that does not compel action or sacrifice. It is a possible starting point for Friendship but does not necessarily mature into it, and it does not arise from motives of advantage or pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affection and intimacy as requirements for true Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Affection requires intensity and intimacy; true Friendship involves yearning and sustained desire for the other's presence, not mere momentary pleasure or superficial liking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship develops from repeated intimacy and mutual concern; mere pleasure in someone's appearance or a transient liking does not constitute Friendship unless it ripens into longing and mutual action on behalf of the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Sentiment (social friendship) vs Unity of Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Sentiment concerns agreement on matters of action and expediency (common choice and conduct) and is linked to Friendship; Unity of Opinion (e.g., on scientific points) does not by itself constitute Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communities or friends exhibit Unity of Sentiment when they agree on practical, important, and mutual interests (e.g., choice of magistrates, alliances). Unity of Sentiment is a form of social Friendship because it coordinates action and aims at shared goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefactors often love their beneficiaries more than vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who confer benefits commonly feel more friendship for the objects of their kindness than the recipients feel toward them, because the benefactor's work is like a creation which he loves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations include: creator-loves-work analogy (artisans/poets love their products), pleasure in acting and recollecting honourable deeds, sense of honour attached to benefaction, and the labour invested by the benefactor making the object more valued by its maker than by the recipient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper (noble) self-love vs reproachable self-love
rubrics_metrics.description: Loving oneself is right when one loves the best part of oneself (the rational/intellectual principle) and seeks the noble (καλὸν); reproachable self-love is the selfish pursuit of wealth, honours, and bodily pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The good man is truly 'self-loving' insofar as he loves and obeys his rational principle, giving himself the most noble goods; popular reproach of self-love targets those gratifying irrational desires. Thus self-love must be defined by which part of the self is loved and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Happy (eudaimon) person needs friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the Happy man needs friends: friends provide objects for benefaction, companionship for the activity of living (which constitutes happiness), and pleasurable contemplation of good actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: happiness is an active working, which is easier and more continuous with friends; the good man enjoys contemplating friends' good actions; friends enable the exercise and improvement of virtue through shared life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number of friends to preserve intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not have exceedingly many friends; the proper number is the greatest with whom one can maintain intimacy, because true Friendship involves deep sympathy that cannot be divided among many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too many friends make requiting kindnesses impracticable and prevent real intimacy. Famous friendships are typically between two persons; broad sociability without intimacy makes one friend to many but truly friend to none.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friends are especially needed in adversity but also valuable in prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: Friends are required in both states: the unfortunate need help (useful friends), and the prosperous need friends for benefaction and honour (good friends). Presence and sympathy of friends comfort in adversity; companionship and shared pleasure are goods in prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical prescriptions: call in friends readily on occasions of good fortune (to do good to others); in bad fortune, be reluctant to impose but seek help when small trouble to friends can yield great aid. Go to friends in their misfortunes unasked and with alacrity; avoid appearing sullen when offered help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimacy (shared activity) is the core of Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Intimacy — shared life and participation in the activities one values (drinking, hunting, study, etc.) — is most choice-worthy for friends; friendship is communion and the desire to share one's chosen way of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through repeated intercourse friends improve one another and learn good from the good (poetic: 'Thou from the good, good things shalt surely learn'). Intimacy also makes friendship productive of moral improvement rather than mutual corruption (which happens among the wicked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure's relation to the good life debated (is Pleasure the Chief Good?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some (Eudoxus) argue Pleasure is the Chief Good because all (rational and irrational) aim at it; others deny this, arguing Pleasure may be only one class of good and not supremely the Chief Good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations include: Pleasure is chosen for itself and seems to augment other goods; Plato's counterargument is that a compound of Pleasure with Practical Wisdom is better than simple Pleasure, which undermines Pleasure's claim to be the Chief Good. The passage recommends balancing theory with facts when forming moral doctrines about Pleasure.
